questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an asset?
questions.why: Salary payable is a liability -- a future sacrifice. Cash, inventory and debtors all have future benefit = assets.

questions.q: The accounting equation is:
questions.why: The fundamental equation: every resource (assets) was funded by outsiders (liabilities) or owners (equity). Both sides must always balance.

questions.q: A company buys a machine for Rs.10L cash. What is the double-entry impact?
questions.why: One asset (cash) converts to another asset (machine). Both impacts on the left side -- net change = zero. Equation stays balanced.

questions.q: Retained Earnings is part of:
questions.why: RE is the second component of Owners Equity (first = Share Capital). It represents accumulated profits kept in the business.

questions.q: Which statement shows performance OVER A PERIOD?
questions.why: The Income Statement covers a period ('for the year ended'). The Balance Sheet is a point-in-time snapshot ('as at'). Frequently tested distinction.

questions.q: A refundable security deposit for a rented showroom is recorded as:
questions.why: The deposit will be returned -- future benefit = Asset. Rent expense is only recorded when the space is actually used (Accrual Concept).

questions.q: Which is a financing activity?
questions.why: Taking a loan = raising funds = financing. Buying machinery = investing. Selling goods and paying salaries = operating.

questions.q: Under the Accrual Concept, expenses are recorded when:
questions.why: Record when incurred (benefit received), not when cash moves.

questions.q: Capital Employed equals:
questions.why: Capital Employed = Net Worth + Long-term Debt. Total funds deployed in the business.

questions.q: Working Capital is:
questions.why: Working Capital = Current Assets minus Current Liabilities. Measures short-term liquidity.

questions.q: Dividends paid appear in the financial statements as:
options: An expense in the Income Statement
A reduction of Retained Earnings in the Balance Sheet
An asset in the Balance Sheet
questions.why: Dividends are not an expense -- not in the P&L.; They reduce Retained Earnings on the Balance Sheet and appear under Financing in the Cash Flow Statement.

questions.q: Under Going Concern, assets are recorded at:
options: Historical cost, depreciated over useful life
questions.why: Going Concern assumes the business will continue -- assets recorded at cost and depreciated over useful life, not at fire-sale value.

questions.q: COGS stands for:
questions.why: COGS = Cost of Goods Sold. Revenue minus COGS = Gross Profit.

questions.q: EBITDA stands for:
options: Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, Amortisation
Earnings Before Income Tax, Dividends and Assets
Equity-Based Interest Tax, Dividends and Allowances
questions.why: EBITDA strips out non-cash charges and financing costs -- useful proxy for operating cash generation.

questions.q: Correct sequence for preparing financial statements:
questions.why: P&L first (Net Income), then RE Statement (closing RE), then Balance Sheet (closing RE flows in). Each feeds the next.

questions.q: Under Straight Line Method, the annual depreciation charge is:
questions.why: SLM: (Cost minus Residual) / Useful Life = same charge every year. WDV gives higher early, lower later.

questions.q: Deferred Tax arises due to:
options: Timing differences between book and taxable profit
questions.why: Timing differences -- typically from different depreciation methods for Companies Act (SLM) vs Income Tax Act (WDV only).

questions.q: Trade Receivables / Debtors are classified as:
questions.why: Money owed by customers for credit sales -- expected within the operating cycle = Current Assets.

questions.q: The Separate Entity Concept means:
options: Each product line is a separate business
Business and owners are financially separate
Each department has its own accounts
questions.why: Business is a separate legal and financial entity. Owner's personal transactions never mix with business transactions.

questions.q: Which is an investing activity?
options: Buying a delivery vehicle for business
questions.why: Buying a long-term asset = investing. Issuing shares = financing. Paying suppliers and collecting from customers = operating.

questions.q: Net Worth equals:
questions.why: Net Worth = Share Capital + Retained Earnings = Owners Equity. The owners' total stake in the business.

questions.q: CWIP stands for:
options: Cost of Wages Including Provident fund
questions.why: Assets under construction -- not yet ready for use. Once commissioned, they move to Fixed Assets and depreciation begins.

questions.q: The Money Measurement Concept means:
questions.why: Only what can be expressed in money terms goes into the accounting books.

questions.q: Revenue Rs.100L, COGS Rs.60L. Gross Profit is:
questions.why: Gross Profit = Revenue minus COGS = Rs.100L minus Rs.60L = Rs.40L.

questions.q: Total Assets Rs.500L, Total Liabilities Rs.320L. Owners Equity is:
questions.why: OE = Assets minus Liabilities = Rs.500L minus Rs.320L = Rs.180L.

questions.q: PBT stands for:
questions.why: PBT = Profit Before Tax. After interest, before income tax. Also called EBT.

questions.q: Which concept divides business life into reporting periods?
questions.why: The Accounting Period Concept -- creates the need for accrual-based accounting.

questions.q: EPS is calculated as:
questions.why: EPS = PAT / Shares outstanding. Measures profit earned per share.

questions.q: Under WDV, depreciation in early years is:
questions.why: WDV front-loads depreciation. Total over the asset's life is the same as SLM -- only timing differs.

questions.q: The Cash Flow Statement has which three sections?
questions.why: Exactly the three business activities: Operating (CFO), Investing (CFI), Financing (CFF).

questions.q: Machinery is a fictitious asset.
questions.why: Machinery is a tangible FIXED ASSET -- real, physical, depreciable.

questions.q: Creditors (trade payables) represent a long-term liability.
questions.why: Suppliers are paid within the operating cycle (typically 60-90 days) -- CURRENT LIABILITY.

questions.q: Investment in a 5-year government bond is always a current asset.
questions.why: Depends on maturity: current if matures within 12 months; non-current otherwise.

questions.q: Salary payable to employees is both an expense and a current liability.
questions.why: Expense (reduces OE) when incurred. Current liability (obligation to pay) if unpaid at period end.

questions.q: Interest on a loan taken is income.
questions.why: Interest PAID on debt taken = finance cost (EXPENSE). Interest EARNED on deposits/investments = income.

questions.q: Share capital is an asset.
questions.why: Share capital is Owners Equity -- a SOURCE of funds on the right side. Not an asset.

questions.q: Interest earned on a mutual fund is an expense.
questions.why: It is INCOME -- other income from an investing activity.

questions.q: Inventory is a non-current asset.
questions.why: Inventory is held for sale within the operating cycle -- CURRENT ASSET.

questions.q: SLM and WDV produce the same TOTAL depreciation over the full life.
questions.why: Total depreciable amount (Cost - Residual) is fixed. Only the ANNUAL ALLOCATION differs.

questions.q: A company can freely switch between SLM and WDV whenever it chooses.
questions.why: Requires strong justification and disclosure to shareholders. Not a routine practice.

questions.q: If Net Book Value reaches zero, the asset must be disposed of.
questions.why: NBV = zero means fully depreciated in books. Physical asset can still be in use -- just stop recording depreciation.

questions.q: Unearned Revenue is a liability.
questions.why: Cash received before service is performed = obligation to perform or refund = LIABILITY until the service is done.

questions.q: A bad debt write-off reverses the original revenue.
questions.why: Original revenue STANDS -- correctly recognised when service was performed. Write-off = new separate expense in the period of write-off.

questions.q: Goodwill on a balance sheet always means the company has done an M&A transaction.
questions.why: Only PURCHASED goodwill is permitted. Arises only when a premium is paid above book value in an actual acquisition.

questions.q: CFO should ideally be higher than Net Income for a healthy business.
questions.why: Depreciation (non-cash) adds back to cash; good collections mean cash comes in faster than accrual revenue.

questions.q: Depreciation is a cash outflow.
questions.why: Non-cash book entry. Cash left when the asset was PURCHASED. Depreciation just spreads that historical cost.

questions.q: A profitable company can go bankrupt.
questions.why: Profit is on accrual. If cash is not collected, a business can run out of money despite reporting paper profits.

questions.q: The Income Tax Act allows both SLM and WDV.
questions.why: Income Tax Act allows ONLY WDV. Companies Act allows both.

questions.q: A change in depreciation estimate (useful life) requires restating prior financial statements.
questions.why: Changes in accounting ESTIMATES are applied PROSPECTIVELY only. No restatement of prior periods.

questions.q: Babu's advance payment to Richie in February should be recorded as February revenue.
questions.why: Cash received does not equal revenue earned. Service not yet done = Unearned Revenue = LIABILITY.

questions.q: Asset costs Rs.11,000 cr, residual Rs.1,000 cr, life 10 years, using SLM. Annual depreciation is:
questions.why: SLM = (Cost - Residual) / Useful Life = (11,000 - 1,000) / 10 = Rs.1,000 cr per year.

questions.q: After 6 years of SLM depreciation (Q1 above), Net Book Value is:
questions.why: NBV = Gross Block - Accumulated Dep = 11,000 - (1,000 x 6) = 11,000 - 6,000 = Rs.5,000 cr.

questions.q: Under WDV, compared to SLM, profit in the EARLY YEARS will be:
options: It depends on the asset type
questions.why: WDV front-loads depreciation. Higher depreciation early = lower profit early. Tax benefit in early years is why companies use WDV for tax.

questions.q: Richie computer: cost Rs.4,68,000, life 36 months, zero residual. Monthly depreciation is:
questions.why: Monthly depreciation = (4,68,000 - 0) / 36 = Rs.13,000.

questions.q: Richie pays Rs.60,000 security deposit for his office. This is recorded as:
questions.why: Refundable deposit = future benefit = ASSET called Security Deposit. Not rent expense.

questions.q: A client pays Rs.4,000 in February for advisory work to be done in March. In February, record:
questions.why: Cash DOES come in = Cash UP. But service not done = Unearned Revenue (LIABILITY). Revenue only when service is performed in March.

questions.q: When the advisory work is done in March (Q6 above), the entry is:
questions.why: The liability (Unearned Revenue) is now discharged because the service is done. Revenue is finally recognised. Cash is not involved (it came in February).

questions.q: Magazine subscription Rs.6,000 for 12 months. After 4 months, Prepaid Expense on balance sheet is:
questions.why: 4 months consumed = Rs.2,000 expense. 8 months remaining = Rs.4,000 Prepaid Expense (asset).

questions.q: Richie performs work for Raghu (Rs.5,000) in February. Raghu vanishes in March. Two-month combined P&L effect is:
options: Zero (revenue in Feb cancels expense in Mar)
questions.why: Feb: +Rs.5,000 revenue. Mar: -Rs.5,000 bad debt expense. Net = zero. Correct economic outcome -- did the work, collected nothing.

questions.q: Richie's February revenue is Rs.20,000. This EXCLUDES:
questions.why: Babu's Rs.4,000 is EXCLUDED from revenue because the service is not done yet. It is Unearned Revenue (liability). The other three ARE revenue in February.

questions.q: Richie's February Net Loss is Rs.74,900. The PRIMARY reason is:
options: Fixed costs (salaries, rent, depreciation) with only Rs.20,000 revenue in a startup month
questions.why: February was setup month. Fixed costs (salaries Rs.50k, rent Rs.20k, depreciation Rs.13k) alone = Rs.83,000 against revenue of only Rs.20,000. Classic startup pattern.

questions.q: In March, Babu's Rs.4,000 converts from Unearned Revenue to Revenue because:
options: Richie received additional payment from Babu
The advisory service was actually performed in March
questions.why: Revenue recognition: ONLY when service is PERFORMED. The time lapse or confirmation does not matter -- performance matters.

questions.q: Richie raises a Rs.5,00,000 bank loan at 12% p.a. in March. March interest expense is:
questions.why: Monthly interest = 5,00,000 x 12% / 12 = Rs.5,000. It is ACCRUED in March (payable April 1st) but recorded as March expense.

questions.q: March interest is not paid until April 1st. The March balance sheet shows:
options: Interest Expense reduces OE + Interest Payable (liability)
questions.why: Accrual concept: interest is INCURRED in March (used the money in March) so recorded as expense and matching liability (Interest Payable) until paid.

questions.q: March revenues grew 11x from February. This proves:
options: The business model is working; volatility brought clients to Richie
February's loss was a strategic error
The financial statements for February were incorrect
questions.why: Richie's thesis was correct: market panic = high advisory demand. February was setup cost. March validated the model.

questions.q: Richie's equipment cost Rs.4,68,000. Half was paid cash, half as Trade Creditor. Cash Flow Statement classification:
options: Rs.2,34,000 in CFI (investing), Rs.2,34,000 in CFF
Rs.2,34,000 in CFI (cash paid for asset). Creditor portion = non-cash, not in CFS
questions.why: Only actual cash movements appear in the Cash Flow Statement. Rs.2,34,000 paid = CFI outflow. The Rs.2,34,000 on credit = non-cash transaction, shown as supplementary disclosure.

questions.q: HPCL shows accounting losses but positive CFO. This is BEST described as:
options: A turnaround signal -- generating real cash despite accounting losses
questions.why: Positive CFO despite accounting loss often means business is operationally sound; accounting loss may be from non-cash charges (large depreciation) or accounting timing differences.

questions.q: Goodwill Rs.200 crore appears on Tata Tea's balance sheet after acquiring Tetley. Tetley's book value was Rs.150 crore. Tata Tea paid:
questions.why: Goodwill = Purchase Price - Book Value. So Purchase Price = Goodwill + Book Value = 200 + 150 = Rs.350 crore.

questions.q: Which of the following is a CURRENT LIABILITY?
options: Advance received from customer for delivery next month
questions.why: Advance from customer = Unearned Revenue = obligation to perform or refund within the next cycle = CURRENT LIABILITY. All others are non-current (long-term).

questions.q: The Indirect Method of computing CFO starts with:
questions.why: Indirect Method: Start with PAT, add back non-cash charges (depreciation), adjust for changes in working capital. Most Indian annual reports use this method.

questions.q: Richie's April services advance of Rs.30,000 received in March is recorded as:
questions.why: Cash received in March but service in April = Unearned Revenue (liability) in March. Revenue only in April when service is performed.

questions.q: A company's Gross Block is Rs.200 crore, Accumulated Depreciation is Rs.75 crore. Net Block is:
questions.why: Net Block = Gross Block - Accumulated Depreciation = 200 - 75 = Rs.125 crore.

questions.q: Which of the following best indicates a company generating strong cash quality?
options: CFO much lower than Net Income
CFO roughly equal to or higher than Net Income
questions.why: CFO >= Net Income signals that reported profits are converting to real cash (good collections, depreciation add-back). CFO much lower than NI = profit quality concern.

questions.q: Company A: Net Income Rs.50L, Depreciation Rs.10L, Debtors decreased Rs.5L. Approximate CFO is:
questions.why: CFO = NI + Dep + Decrease in Debtors = 50 + 10 + 5 = Rs.65L. Debtors decreasing means cash was collected (adds to cash).

questions.q: The Misra Company's net profit margin fell from 5% to 3.1%. After reviewing the multi-step P&L, the correct decision is:
options: Identify whether the fall is from a one-time non-recurring item before drawing conclusions
questions.why: Multi-step P&L revealed the entire fall was one-time loss on asset disposal (investing decision). Always decompose the journey from operating profit to net profit before concluding.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about changing a depreciation method?
options: Companies can change freely every year to reduce tax
Requires strong justification and disclosure; not allowed as a routine practice
Must be approved by the government
Changes must be applied retrospectively (restate all prior years)
questions.why: Strong justification + disclosure required. Changes in accounting ESTIMATES (like useful life) apply prospectively. Not a routine practice.

questions.q: A company uses SLM for its published accounts but WDV for its tax return. In early years, this creates:
options: Higher published profit, lower taxable profit -- and a Deferred Tax Liability
Lower published profit, higher taxable profit
questions.why: WDV gives higher depreciation early = lower taxable profit = less tax now. SLM gives lower depreciation early = higher published profit. Tax saved today will reverse later = Deferred Tax Liability (DTL).

questions.q: Assets remaining useful beyond their fully depreciated NBV should be:
options: Continued in use with no further depreciation charge
questions.why: When NBV reaches zero (or residual value), simply STOP recording depreciation. Asset continues in use. It is "free" in accounting terms.

questions.q: Richie's February balance sheet shows Cash Rs.6,50,000. Which transaction contributed Rs.4,000 to this cash that students often miss?
options: Babu's advance (cash came in despite being Unearned Revenue)
questions.why: Babu's Rs.4,000 IS a cash inflow in February -- it physically arrives in the bank. But it is classified as Unearned Revenue (LIABILITY) because the service is not done. Cash in = yes. Revenue = no.

questions.q: Two companies with identical revenues. Company A has COGS 80% of sales, Company B has COGS 55%. Who has more pricing power?
options: Company A -- higher costs mean higher quality
Company B -- retains more per rupee of sales after direct costs
Both the same -- revenue is equal
Cannot determine without knowing absolute profit
questions.why: Gross margin: A = 20%, B = 45%. B retains significantly more after direct costs -- better pricing, lower input costs, or more efficient production.

questions.q: A machine is purchased for Rs.5,00,000. Installation cost Rs.50,000. Transport Rs.25,000. The COST for depreciation purposes is:
questions.why: Cost = ALL expenditure to get the asset ready for use: purchase + installation + transport = 5,00,000 + 50,000 + 25,000 = Rs.5,75,000.

questions.q: Which statement about the Balance Sheet is FALSE?
options: It is prepared at a specific point in time
Total Assets always equal Total Liabilities plus Owners Equity
It shows how much profit was earned during the year
It shows what the company owns and what it owes
questions.why: Profit earned DURING the year is shown on the INCOME STATEMENT. The balance sheet shows the financial POSITION at a specific DATE -- a snapshot, not a movie.

questions.q: Richie's March cumulative net income over two months is Rs.17,200. This means shareholders who invested Rs.10,00,000:
options: Have owners equity of Rs.10,17,200 -- slightly ahead of their investment
questions.why: Owners equity = Share Capital (Rs.10,00,000) + Retained Earnings (Rs.17,200) = Rs.10,17,200. Higher than invested. Business model validated in 2 months.

questions.q: Which goes in CFI (Investing activities) in Richie's Cash Flow Statement?
questions.why: Computer hardware = long-term asset (3+ years) = INVESTING activity. All others = operating.

questions.q: Interest paid by Richie on his bank loan is classified under which section in Indian GAAP (AS 3)?
options: Not classified -- it is a non-cash expense
questions.why: For a non-financial company, both AS 3 (Indian GAAP) and Ind AS 7 classify interest paid under financing activities (CFF); interest and dividends received go under investing. Only financial enterprises such as banks show them under operating. (Corrected from the original notes, which said CFO.)

questions.q: Total fixed cost stays constant regardless of production volume.
questions.why: By definition. Same Rs.50,000 rent whether 100 or 1,000 units are produced.

questions.q: Fixed cost per unit stays constant as volume rises.
questions.why: Fixed TOTAL is constant. Per-unit fixed cost FALLS as more units spread the same fixed total.

questions.q: Variable cost per unit rises as you produce more.
questions.why: Variable cost PER UNIT is CONSTANT. Only the total rises proportionally with volume.

questions.q: Management accounting is regulated by ICAI like financial accounting.
questions.why: No regulation, no standard format. For internal use only.

questions.q: A cost object must always be a physical product.
questions.why: A cost object can be a product, batch, programme, department, project, or customer.

questions.q: Direct costs always need a cost driver to be allocated.
questions.why: Direct costs are TRACED, not allocated. Only INDIRECT costs need a driver.

questions.q: Contribution margin is Revenue minus all Fixed Costs.
questions.why: Contribution = Revenue minus all VARIABLE COSTS. Fixed costs come after contribution.

questions.q: A business can have positive contribution margin and still make a net loss.
questions.why: If total fixed costs exceed total contribution, the business is below break-even -- loss despite positive CM.

questions.q: Beyond break-even, each extra unit contributes its full selling price to profit.
questions.why: Beyond BEP, each unit contributes its CONTRIBUTION MARGIN (price minus variable cost), not full price.

questions.q: CS Ratio = 40% means 40 paise of every rupee of sales is contribution.
questions.why: CS Ratio = Contribution / Sales. Exactly what it means.

questions.q: Margin of safety = current sales minus TARGET sales.
questions.why: MOS = Current Sales minus BREAK-EVEN Sales. Target is not involved.

questions.q: A product with a LOWER margin of safety ratio is LESS risky.
questions.why: Lower MOS = closer to break-even = MORE risky, not less.

questions.q: For multi-product BEP, use a simple average of all product contributions.
questions.why: Use a WEIGHTED AVERAGE with sales mix proportions. Simple average ignores relative volumes.

questions.q: The high-low method assumes a linear cost-volume relationship.
questions.why: It draws a straight line between two data points. Non-linear behaviour produces only an approximation.

questions.q: Depreciation is a relevant cost when deciding to shut down a subsidiary.
questions.why: Depreciation is non-cash. Equipment already bought. Closing saves nothing on depreciation. IRRELEVANT.

questions.q: A non-cancelable lease is irrelevant to the shutdown decision.
questions.why: Paid regardless -- same cost in every scenario. Irrelevant to the shutdown choice.

questions.q: A client at $500/hr should be rejected if the standard price is $800/hr.
questions.why: If the machine is otherwise idle, ANY price above variable cost ($28/hr) generates contribution. $500 passes easily.

questions.q: Contribution analysis requires the income statement in traditional format.
questions.why: Traditional format MIXES fixed and variable. Need the contribution format with costs split by BEHAVIOUR.

questions.q: Period costs are capitalised as inventory until the product is sold.
questions.why: PRODUCT costs are capitalised. Period costs go DIRECTLY to the income statement -- no inventory detour.

questions.q: Manufacturing overhead can include both fixed and variable components.
questions.why: Supervisor salary (fixed), factory electricity (partly variable), equipment insurance (fixed) -- all overhead.

questions.q: Which of the following is a DIRECT cost for a computer manufacturer?
options: Processor chips used in each computer
questions.why: Processor chips physically become part of each computer -- directly traceable = DIRECT COST. Factory supervisor, rent, and electricity benefit multiple products = INDIRECT (overhead).

questions.q: Factory electricity is Rs.5,000/month fixed standing charge plus Rs.2/unit consumed. This is a:
questions.why: Fixed component (Rs.5,000) + variable component (Rs.2/unit) = MIXED COST. Must be split before CVP analysis.

questions.q: Product A costs Rs.800 per unit to make, selling price Rs.1,200. Fixed costs Rs.4,00,000. Break-even units:
Using Q3 data: CS Ratio is:
questions.why: CS Ratio = CM / Selling Price = 400 / 1,200 = 33.3%. Approximately 33%.

questions.q: Using Q3 data: Break-even SALES VALUE is:
questions.why: BEP Sales = Fixed Costs / CS Ratio = 4,00,000 / (1/3) = Rs.12,00,000. Check: 1,000 units x Rs.1,200 = Rs.12,00,000.

questions.q: Using Q3 data: how many units to earn Rs.1,00,000 target profit?
Using Q3 data: current sales are 1,200 units. Margin of Safety in units is:
questions.why: MOS = Current - BEP = 1,200 - 1,000 = 200 units.

questions.q: Using Q3 data: current profit at 1,200 units (using MOS shortcut):
Fixed costs rise from Rs.4,00,000 to Rs.4,80,000. New break-even units (CM unchanged at Rs.400):
questions.why: New BEP = 4,80,000 / 400 = 1,200 units. Every Rs.80,000 rise in fixed costs requires 200 more units just to break even.

questions.q: The contribution income statement differs from the traditional income statement because:
options: It shows Gross Profit instead of Contribution Margin
Costs are separated by BEHAVIOUR (fixed vs variable) not FUNCTION (production vs overhead)
It is only for external reporting
questions.why: Traditional = costs by function. Contribution = costs by behaviour (all variable then all fixed). Only contribution format enables CVP analysis.

questions.q: A company operates at 60% capacity with profit of Rs.2,00,000 and FC of Rs.8,00,000. CM is:
questions.why: Profit = CM - FC. So CM = Profit + FC = 2,00,000 + 8,00,000 = Rs.10,00,000.

questions.q: The high-low method: January power cost $1,633 (361 hrs), February $1,592 (348 hrs). Variable rate per hour:
questions.why: Using Jan-Feb pair: (1,633 - 1,592) / (361 - 348) = 41 / 13 = $3.15/hr. However, the Prestige class answer is $4/hr, derived by averaging all three available data pairs. If asked for Prestige specifically, use $4/hr.

questions.q: Using Q12: Fixed power cost per month is approximately:
questions.why: Using the $4/hr class answer: Fixed = Total cost - (Variable rate x hours) = 1,633 - (4 x 361) = 1,633 - 1,444 = $189 approximately $200/month.

questions.q: Prestige Data Services: commercial rate $800/hr, variable cost $28/hr. Contribution per commercial hour:
questions.why: Commercial CM/hr = $800 - $28 = $772. Every commercial hour throws $772 toward fixed costs.

questions.q: Prestige: total fixed costs $213,000, intracompany contribution $76,260/month. Remaining fixed cost gap:
questions.why: Gap = Total FC - Intracompany contribution = 213,000 - 76,260 = $136,740. This gap must be covered by commercial hours.

questions.q: Prestige break-even commercial hours: gap $136,740, commercial CM $772/hr:
questions.why: BEP commercial = $136,740 / $772 = 177 hours/month.

questions.q: Prestige Option C: marketing increases commercial hours from 132 to 172 at $800/hr. Max marketing budget that still improves profit:
questions.why: Extra contribution = 40 extra hours x $772 = $30,880. Any marketing spend below $30,880 would improve profit. Above $30,880 = worse off.

questions.q: Which Prestige option is the WORST choice?
questions.why: Option D reduces commercial hours by 20% (to 106) with barely any cost saving. Loss worsens by ~$18,000. Worst outcome.

questions.q: An idle machine can process client orders at $500/hr. Variable cost $28/hr. Should Richie accept this order?
options: Yes -- any price above variable cost generates contribution when machine is idle
Only if the client agrees to long-term contract
No -- it sets a bad price precedent
questions.why: When the machine is IDLE, the relevant comparison is: price vs variable cost. $500 > $28. Contribution = $472/hr. ACCEPT. Standard price irrelevant for idle capacity decisions.

questions.q: Product Cost vs Period Cost: Rs.2,000 advertising expense for a product that partly remains unsold. Advertising hits the P&L:
options: Only when the product is sold (proportionally)
Immediately in full, regardless of units sold
questions.why: Advertising = PERIOD COST. Hits P&L IMMEDIATELY in full. NOT apportioned between sold and unsold units.

questions.q: Manufacturing overhead includes which of the following?
questions.why: Factory supervisor salary is an INDIRECT MANUFACTURING cost = part of Manufacturing Overhead (Box 3). Sales commissions, CEO salary, advertising = PERIOD COSTS.

questions.q: Company spends Rs.5L making 1,000 units. Sells 700 units at Rs.800 each. COGS on P&L is:
questions.why: Cost per unit = Rs.500. 700 units sold x Rs.500 = Rs.3,50,000 COGS on P&L.; Rs.1,50,000 remains as inventory (asset).

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE about the contribution margin?
options: Contribution per unit = Selling Price - Variable Cost per unit
questions.why: CM per unit = P - V. It is what each unit contributes toward covering fixed costs and then profit. Can be zero or negative if price < variable cost.

questions.q: Product X: Selling price Rs.200, variable cost Rs.150, FC Rs.50,000. Currently selling 800 units. Proposal: reduce price to Rs.180 and increase volume to 1,000 units. Net impact on profit:
questions.why: Current CM = (200-150)x800 = 40,000. Proposed CM = (180-150)x1,000 = 30,000. Fixed costs same. Net change in profit = 30,000-40,000 = -Rs.10,000. Proposed situation is worse.

questions.q: Multi-product: Product A (CM Rs.100, 600 units) and Product B (CM Rs.200, 400 units). Weighted CM is:
Using Q25 data: Fixed costs Rs.1,40,000. Break-even combined units:
questions.why: BEP = 1,40,000 / 140 = 1,000 combined units.

questions.q: Prestige's depreciation of Rs.26,180/month is IRRELEVANT to the shutdown decision because:
options: It is too small to matter
It is a non-cash charge and the equipment is already purchased -- closing saves nothing
It is paid to the parent company
questions.why: Non-cash, sunk cost. Whether open or closed, depreciation runs on already-purchased equipment. IRRELEVANT to any forward-looking decision.

questions.q: Total fixed costs are Rs.3,00,000/month. CS ratio is 30%. Break-even sales value:
questions.why: BEP Sales = FC / CS Ratio = 3,00,000 / 0.30 = Rs.10,00,000.

questions.q: At break-even point, the margin of safety is:
questions.why: At BEP: Current sales = Break-even sales. MOS = Current - BEP = zero. You are exactly at the edge -- one unit below = loss.

questions.q: A company's profit is Rs.60,000 and CS ratio is 40%. Margin of Safety SALES value is:
questions.why: Profit = MOS Sales x CS Ratio. So MOS Sales = Profit / CS = 60,000 / 0.40 = Rs.1,50,000.

questions.q: Which cost is RELEVANT to a make-vs-buy decision?
options: Avoidable labour and material cost if buying externally
Head office rent that continues regardless
questions.why: Relevant costs = future, avoidable, differential. Avoidable labour/material if you buy externally = relevant. Depreciation and head office rent = unavoidable = irrelevant.

questions.q: Fixed costs per unit FALL as production volume RISES. This explains:
options: The economic logic of economies of scale
Why break-even is different for every company
questions.why: Fixed costs spread over more units = lower fixed cost per unit = lower total cost per unit = ECONOMIES OF SCALE.

questions.q: Prestige intracompany rate is $400/hr. Commercial rate is $800/hr. Both have variable cost $28/hr. Intracompany CM vs Commercial CM:
questions.why: CM = Price - Variable Cost. Intracompany: $400-$28=$372. Commercial: $800-$28=$772. Commercial generates $400 more contribution per hour.

questions.q: Rowe should NOT shut Prestige Data Services in April 2003 because:
options: The subsidiary is profitable on paper
The unavoidable fixed costs (lease, depreciation, rent) keep running after closure but revenue disappears
questions.why: Relevant cost analysis: close = lose ALL revenue (~$200k+) but keep unavoidable costs (~$130k). Net impact of closing = WORSE.

questions.q: Variable cost per unit is Rs.50. Selling price is Rs.120. Target profit is Rs.2,00,000. Fixed costs are Rs.1,00,000. Units required:
Trend analysis can use any convenient year as the base year.
questions.why: Base year = Year 1 ALWAYS. Any other choice loses data points unnecessarily.

questions.q: Vertical analysis removes the size bias between companies.
questions.why: Common-sizing sets the anchor to 100% -- absolute size becomes irrelevant to comparison.

questions.q: A bonus issue increases Total Owner's Equity.
questions.why: SC up and RE down by the SAME AMOUNT. Total OE is COMPLETELY UNCHANGED.

questions.q: Bonus shares benefit shareholders via unlocking of shareholder wealth.
questions.why: Positive confidence signal drives demand and price above the mathematical split.

questions.q: Stock splits and bonus issues produce broadly similar economic outcomes.
questions.why: Different mechanics (face value vs reserves), but market effects are broadly similar.

questions.q: A buyback is motivated by a desire to gain management control.
questions.why: Correct motivation: shares are undervalued and the company has available cash.

questions.q: In a buyback, the full purchase price reduces Share Capital.
questions.why: Face value reduces SC. The PREMIUM over face value reduces Reserves and Surplus.

questions.q: Higher current ratio always signals better financial health.
questions.why: Excess liquidity = idle capital in low-return assets. Higher is NOT always better.

questions.q: HUL's negative working capital signals financial stress.
questions.why: It signals market power -- collects before it pays. A STRENGTH, not a weakness.

questions.q: Inventory is excluded from Quick Ratio because it generates no return.
questions.why: Excluded because it may NOT convert to cash quickly in a downturn.

questions.q: Days Payable Outstanding should be minimised for best efficiency.
questions.why: DPO should be MAXIMISED within agreed terms -- pay as late as possible.

questions.q: Cash Conversion Cycle = DIO + DSO + DPO.
questions.why: Correct: DIO + DSO MINUS DPO. Longer payables REDUCE the cycle.

questions.q: COGS is the correct numerator for Inventory Turnover.
questions.why: Inventory is held at cost -- COGS is the matching metric.

questions.q: ROTA will always be higher than ROE for the same business.
questions.why: ROE has a smaller denominator (equity only) -- ROE is typically HIGHER.

questions.q: Debt is cheaper than equity because lenders face lower risk.
questions.why: Lenders have priority claim in liquidation; equity is residual and riskier. Lower risk = lower required return.

questions.q: A debt-free company is always better for shareholders.
questions.why: If ROTA > cost of debt, leverage AMPLIFIES ROE. Debt-free forgoes this genuine benefit.

questions.q: Interest Coverage of 1.0 means the business is in trouble.
questions.why: EBIT barely covers interest. No buffer for principal, tax, or any operating downturn.

questions.q: Horizontal analysis works column by column down the statement.
questions.why: Horizontal works ROW BY ROW -- comparing the same line item across DIFFERENT PERIODS.

questions.q: Ratio analysis is the primary PURPOSE of financial statements.
questions.why: Statements are for reporting. Ratio analysis is the USER'S tool applied on top of them.

questions.q: A common-sized balance sheet can reveal the industry of an anonymous company.
questions.why: IT, manufacturing, banking, FMCG all have distinctive asset and liability profiles visible in common-size format.

questions.q: Company ABC: SC Rs.250 cr, Reserves Rs.750 cr, 25 cr shares. A 1:2 bonus (1 bonus for every 2 held) is announced. Post-bonus Share Capital is:
questions.why: 1:2 bonus = add 50% more shares. New shares = 25 x 50% = 12.5 cr at face value Rs.10 = Rs.125 cr added to SC. New SC = 250 + 125 = Rs.375 cr. Reserves fall by Rs.125 cr.

questions.q: In a stock split of 2:1 (each share splits into 2), Total Owners Equity:
questions.why: Stock split: face value halved, shares doubled. SC total = same. Reserves = same. Total OE = unchanged.

questions.q: A company buys back 1,000 shares at Rs.150 each (face value Rs.10 each). Impact on Reserves and Surplus:
options: Decreases by Rs.1,40,000 (premium above face value)
questions.why: Face value portion (1,000 x Rs.10 = Rs.10,000) reduces Share Capital. Premium (1,000 x Rs.140 = Rs.1,40,000) reduces Reserves and Surplus. Total cash out = Rs.1,50,000.

questions.q: Year 1 Net Revenue = Rs.100 cr. Year 3 = Rs.145 cr. Year 5 = Rs.230 cr. Trend index for Year 5 is:
questions.why: Trend index = (Value / Base Year 1 Value) x 100 = (230/100) x 100 = 230. Base year (Year 1) = 100 always.

questions.q: Starbucks: Revenues grew 20.9%, Cost of Sales grew 25.8%. What does horizontal analysis reveal?
options: Cost of production is growing faster than revenue -- margin pressure
The company is over-invested in assets
questions.why: Cost growing faster than revenue = gross margin falling. Even though absolute revenue grew, the business retained less per rupee of sales. Action needed on cost structure.

questions.q: A common-size balance sheet shows Company X with Inventory 18% of total assets and Company Y with Inventory 0.1%. Company Y is most likely:
options: An IT services or consulting firm
questions.why: IT/consulting = no physical inventory. Knowledge-based businesses have near-zero inventory.

questions.q: Current Assets Rs.80L, Current Liabilities Rs.50L, Inventory Rs.20L. Quick Ratio is:
questions.why: Quick Ratio = (CA - Inventory) / CL = (80 - 20) / 50 = 60/50 = 1.2.

questions.q: Current Assets Rs.60L, Current Liabilities Rs.80L. Working Capital is:
questions.why: WC = CA - CL = 60 - 80 = -Rs.20L. NEGATIVE working capital. May indicate market power (like HUL) or liquidity concern -- context determines which.

questions.q: Company A Current Ratio = 3.5. Company B Current Ratio = 1.3 (same industry). Better investment is likely:
options: Company B -- leaner, more capital deployed productively
questions.why: Current ratio 3.5 means significant idle capital in low-return assets. Company B (1.3) has more capital in productive assets.

questions.q: Sales Rs.500 cr, Avg Inventory Rs.50 cr, COGS Rs.350 cr. Inventory Turnover is:
questions.why: Inventory Turnover = COGS / Avg Inventory = 350 / 50 = 7 times. Use COGS (not revenue) because inventory is valued at cost.

questions.q: Using Q10 data: Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) is approximately:
questions.why: DIO = 365 / Inventory Turnover = 365 / 7 = 52.1 approximately 52 days.

questions.q: Debtors Turnover = 8 times, Creditors Turnover = 6 times, Inventory Turnover = 10 times. CCC is:
questions.why: DIO = 365/10 = 36.5, DSO = 365/8 = 45.6, DPO = 365/6 = 60.8. CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO = 36.5 + 45.6 - 60.8 = 21.3 approximately 21 days (closest option = 24 days).

questions.q: Gross Profit Rs.40L, Sales Rs.100L. Gross Profit Margin is:
questions.why: GPM = (Gross Profit / Sales) x 100 = (40/100) x 100 = 40%.

questions.q: Operating Profit Rs.20L, Sales Rs.100L. Operating Profit Margin is:
PAT Rs.15L, Sales Rs.100L. Net Profit Margin is:
Total Assets Rs.200L, PAT Rs.20L, Interest Rs.5L, Tax Rate 30%. ROTA is approximately:
questions.why: PBIAT = PAT + [Interest x (1 - Tax Rate)] = 20 + [5 x 0.7] = 20 + 3.5 = Rs.23.5L. ROTA = 23.5 / 200 x 100 = 11.75% approximately 12%.

questions.q: Capital Employed Rs.100L, Operating Profit Rs.18L. ROCE is:
questions.why: ROCE = (Operating Profit / Capital Employed) x 100 = 18/100 x 100 = 18%.

questions.q: Net Worth Rs.50L, PAT Rs.10L. ROE is:
questions.why: ROE = (PAT / Net Worth) x 100 = (10/50) x 100 = 20%.

questions.q: EBIT Rs.30L, Interest Rs.5L. Interest Coverage Ratio is:
questions.why: Interest Coverage = (PBT + Interest) / Interest = (25 + 5) / 5 = 30/5 = 6 times.

questions.q: Long-term Debt Rs.60L, Equity Rs.40L. Debt-Equity ratio is:
questions.why: D/E = Long-term Debt / Equity = 60 / 40 = 1.5.

questions.q: ROTA = 14%, cost of debt = 10%. Adding more debt will:
questions.why: ROTA (14%) > Cost of Debt (10%) = positive leverage. Borrowing at 10%, earning 14% on assets = difference flows to equity holders as higher ROE.

questions.q: Govind held 100 shares at Rs.100 each (Rs.10,000 investment). After 1:1 bonus, shares at Rs.70. His wealth change is:
questions.why: Post-bonus: 200 shares x Rs.70 = Rs.14,000. Original investment = Rs.10,000. Gain = Rs.4,000. Market settled at Rs.70 (not mathematical Rs.50) due to confidence signal.

questions.q: Which metric tells you how quickly a company can pay off its interest from earnings?
questions.why: Interest Coverage = EBIT / Interest. Tells how many times current earnings can cover the interest bill. Close to 1.0 = danger zone.

questions.q: Amazon imposes 90-day payment terms on sellers. This is reflected as:
options: High DPO -- Amazon pays late, using sellers' money
High DSO -- Amazon gives long credit
questions.why: Amazon's market power = suppliers cannot push back on long payment terms. High DPO = negative CCC = suppliers funding Amazon's operations.

questions.q: Year 1 Operating Income index = 100. Year 5 = 285. Revenue index Year 5 = 230. This means:
options: Costs are growing faster than revenue
Operating income is growing faster than revenue -- improving margin
Revenue and costs are growing equally
The company is taking on more debt
questions.why: Operating Income index (285) > Revenue index (230). Profit growing faster than sales = improving profitability per rupee of sales.

questions.q: Company X common-size: Fixed Assets 65% of total assets, Debt 55% of capital. Company Y: Fixed Assets 5%, Debt 0%. Most likely industries:
options: X = IT services, Y = Power utility
X = Power utility, Y = IT services
questions.why: Power utility = massive fixed assets (transmission lines, equipment), high debt needed for infrastructure. IT services = asset-light (people), near-zero debt.

questions.q: Which statement about DPO is CORRECT?
options: Lower DPO is always better for the buyer
Higher DPO means the buyer is paying suppliers too slowly
Higher DPO means the buyer is using supplier credit efficiently (free financing)
DPO has no impact on working capital
questions.why: Higher DPO = stretching supplier credit = free funding from suppliers = reduces net cash needed. Within agreed terms, higher is better for the buyer.

questions.q: Profitability on INVESTMENT ratios use which denominator?
options: Various asset/capital measures (Total Assets, Capital Employed, or Equity)
questions.why: Return on Total Assets uses Total Assets. ROCE uses Capital Employed (NW + LT Debt). ROE uses Net Worth (equity only). All three have the same numerator -- profit -- but different denominators.

questions.q: Interest Coverage = 5.0 means:
options: The company can service its debt 5 times over from current earnings
questions.why: IC = EBIT / Interest = 5.0. EBIT can cover interest 5 times over. Comfortable buffer. IC close to 1.0 = barely covering interest = distress signal.

questions.q: Horizontal analysis of Infosys: Revenue +12%, COGS +8%, Operating Expenses +15%. Quick conclusion:
options: All trends are positive -- good company
Revenue growing healthily; COGS controlled; but operating expenses growing faster than revenue -- needs attention
questions.why: Revenue 12% > COGS 8% = good (improving gross margin). But Operating Expenses 15% > Revenue 12% = operating margin pressure. Drill down: which operating expense is growing fastest?

questions.q: A buyback is done at Rs.500/share when management believes fair value is Rs.650/share. This is:
options: A good use of cash -- buying undervalued shares at a discount to fair value
questions.why: If management believes Rs.650 is fair value but shares trade at Rs.500, buying at Rs.500 = buying Rs.650 of value for Rs.500 = excellent investment for remaining shareholders.

questions.q: The FOUR Windows of ratio analysis in correct multiplier order:
questions.why: The logical sequence: LIQUIDITY (survive short-term) enables EFFICIENCY (assets work hard) which generates PROFITABILITY (sales become profit) amplified by LEVERAGE (into higher equity returns).

questions.q: ROE > ROCE > ROTA. This is observed when:
options: ROTA is less than cost of debt
ROTA is greater than cost of debt (positive leverage)
questions.why: When business earns more on assets (ROTA) than debt costs, the surplus flows to equity holders alone (smaller denominator) amplifying ROE above ROCE above ROTA.

questions.q: A vertical analysis balance sheet shows Debt 0%, Investments 40% of assets. This company most likely:
options: Is a startup with high growth needs
Is a mature company with surplus cash and strong operational cash flows, no need for debt
questions.why: Zero debt + high investments = generating cash well beyond operational needs. Likely mature, cash-generative business like TCS or Infosys.

questions.q: Which ratio would BEST tell you whether a company's operations can cover its full debt repayment (principal + interest)?
questions.why: DSCR = Operating CF After Tax / (Interest + Principal Repayment). Tells whether operational cash can fully service all debt obligations -- the most comprehensive debt repayment measure.

questions.q: Which of the following events is NOT recorded in the accounting system?
options: Signing an employment contract (before work begins)
questions.why: Signing a contract has no financial impact yet. Record when value is exchanged, not when contracts are signed.

questions.q: A company buys goods on credit Rs.50,000. Cash has not moved. The TWO impacts are:
questions.why: Goods received = Inventory UP (asset). Payment not made = Trade Payables UP (liability). Cash unchanged.

questions.q: A company earns Rs.80L revenue, incurs Rs.55L expenses. Dividends paid Rs.5L. Closing RE (opening was Rs.10L):
questions.why: Net Income = 80-55=25L. RE = Opening 10 + NI 25 - Dividends 5 = Rs.30L.

questions.q: Which financial statement would you read FIRST to understand HOW a company performed in a year?
questions.why: P&L = performance over the period. Balance Sheet = position at a date. Cash Flow = cash movements. P&L first, always.

questions.q: Assets Rs.500L, Liabilities Rs.320L, Net Income Rs.40L (included in OE), Dividends Rs.10L. Share Capital is:
questions.why: OE = 500-320=180. OE = SC + RE. RE = NI - Dividends = 40-10=30. SC = OE - RE = 180-30=Rs.150L.

questions.q: Machinery Rs.10L, 5-year life, Rs.1L residual, SLM. Net Book Value after 3 years:
questions.why: Annual dep = (10-1)/5 = Rs.1.8L per year. After 3 years: accumulated dep = 1.8 x 3 = Rs.5.4L. NBV = 10 - 5.4 = Rs.4.6L.

questions.q: Which of the following is a NON-CASH expense?
questions.why: Depreciation = book entry only. Cash left when asset was PURCHASED. No cash movement when depreciation is recorded.

questions.q: The Accrual Concept requires recording Rs.20,000 January rent as an expense when:
options: The cash is paid on February 1st
The office is occupied and benefit is consumed in January
questions.why: Record when INCURRED (benefit consumed) = January. Cash timing is irrelevant for expense recognition.

questions.q: A company's CFO is Rs.60L, CFI is -Rs.80L, CFF is Rs.30L. Closing cash (opening Rs.20L):
questions.why: Net change = 60-80+30=+10L. Closing cash = 20+10=Rs.30L.

questions.q: A company reports Rs.100L profit but CFO is Rs.20L. The gap is BEST explained by:
options: Significant credit sales not yet collected, large non-cash charges, or heavy investing
questions.why: Profit (accrual) vs cash is always different. Large gap = significant debtors (sales not collected), depreciation add-back, or investing activities.

questions.q: A company's Gross Profit Margin is 40%, Operating Profit Margin is 15%, Net Profit Margin is 10%. Interest and tax together consume what % of sales?
questions.why: OPM 15% - NPM 10% = 5% consumed by interest + tax. GPM 40% to OPM 15% = 25% = operating expenses.

questions.q: Infosys vs a steel manufacturer. Common-size: which company has near-ZERO inventory?
options: Infosys (IT services) -- provides knowledge/services, not physical goods
questions.why: IT services = no physical product = near-zero inventory.

questions.q: A company retains 60% of its PAT every year (payout ratio 40%). This is BEST for shareholders when:
options: The company needs cash for dividends
The company can invest retained earnings at returns ABOVE what shareholders could earn elsewhere
questions.why: Retaining earnings makes sense if ROTA > shareholders' required return. Otherwise, return it as dividends.

questions.q: Revenue recognition: a software company signs a Rs.12L annual support contract on October 1st. Revenue in Year 1 (ending March 31st):
questions.why: Accrual: recognise revenue as service is PERFORMED. October 1 to March 31 = 6 months. Revenue = 12L x 6/12 = Rs.6L.

questions.q: A company's Capital Employed is Rs.200L and ROCE is 18%. Its Operating Profit is:
questions.why: ROCE = OP / CE. OP = ROCE x CE = 18% x 200 = Rs.36L.

questions.q: Purchased Goodwill is different from internally-generated goodwill because:
options: Purchased goodwill arises from an actual M&A transaction with a verifiable price (objective measurement)
questions.why: Money Measurement Concept: only record what can be objectively measured. M&A = actual transaction = objective price = allowed on balance sheet.

questions.q: A manager asks: "What will our profit be if we sell 500 more units next month?" This CANNOT be answered from:
options: The traditional income statement (which mixes fixed and variable by function)
questions.why: Traditional format mixes fixed and variable in COGS and in Selling & Admin. You cannot isolate how much cost changes with 500 more units.

questions.q: TTK Inc: closing OE = Rs.2,60,000, opening OE = Rs.1,60,000, new share capital Rs.40,000, dividends Rs.48,000. Net Income is:
Which item in the Balance Sheet is the BRIDGE connecting it to the Income Statement?
questions.why: Retained Earnings = Profits accumulated over time. P&L feeds NI into RE. RE sits on the Balance Sheet. Without RE, the balance sheet cannot balance.

questions.q: Going Concern is violated when:
options: The company reports a loss for one year
The company's CFO is temporarily negative
The business intends to cease operations or is forced to liquidate
questions.why: Going Concern = assume business continues. If the business IS shutting down, assets must be valued at liquidation prices (much lower), not historical cost minus depreciation.

questions.q: Variable cost per unit is Rs.80. Selling price Rs.200. FC Rs.2,40,000. Break-even in sales rupees:
Using Q21: current sales Rs.5,00,000. Margin of Safety is:
Using Q21: current profit is:
FC Rs.5,00,000, CM/unit Rs.25, target profit Rs.2,50,000. Units required:
A factory has FC Rs.10L and produces 10,000 units. FC per unit = Rs.10. If production doubles to 20,000 units:
options: FC per unit rises to Rs.20
FC per unit falls to Rs.5
questions.why: Fixed TOTAL stays Rs.10L. But per unit = Rs.10L / 20,000 = Rs.5. Fixed cost per unit HALVES as volume doubles.

questions.q: A company's CS ratio is 35%. At current sales, MOS ratio is 20%. Net profit margin is:
questions.why: Profit % = MOS ratio x CS ratio = 20% x 35% = 7% of sales.

questions.q: Prestige commercial hours: Jan=123, Feb=135, Mar=138. Average growth per month is approximately:
questions.why: From 123 to 138 over 2 months = 15 hours in 2 months = 7.5 hours/month average growth.

questions.q: At Prestige, Option B (reduce price to $600) produces only marginal worsening. This means:
options: The volume increase from lower price almost fully compensates the price cut
Fixed costs should be reduced first
questions.why: Volume increase (30% more hours) x lower CM approximately equals current contribution. Near-neutral.

questions.q: A company accepts a special order at Rs.150/unit when standard price is Rs.200/unit. Variable cost Rs.90/unit. The company has spare capacity. This decision is:
options: Wrong -- always sell at standard price
Right -- contribution of Rs.60/unit is positive and helps cover fixed costs
questions.why: With spare capacity, the relevant comparison is price vs variable cost. Rs.150 > Rs.90 = Rs.60 contribution per unit. ACCEPT.

questions.q: Which cost is IRRELEVANT to ALL future decisions?
options: Sunk costs (already spent, cannot be recovered)
questions.why: Sunk costs are past, irrecoverable. They are IDENTICAL in all future scenarios = irrelevant to decisions.

questions.q: High-low: December power $1,850 (480 hrs), June power $1,250 (180 hrs). Variable rate per hour:
Using Q31: Fixed power cost per month:
questions.why: Fixed = Total cost - (Variable rate x Hours) = 1,250 - (2 x 180) = 1,250 - 360 = $890/month.

questions.q: A factory shuts down for a week. Which cost is ZERO during shutdown?
questions.why: Raw material is consumed ONLY when producing. Zero production = zero raw material consumed. Rent, salaries, and depreciation continue regardless.

questions.q: Product mix: 60% Product A (CM Rs.80/unit), 40% Product B (CM Rs.120/unit). Weighted CM:
A company currently loses Rs.5L per month on a division. Avoidable costs = Rs.3L/month. Unavoidable costs = Rs.4L/month. Revenue = Rs.2L/month. Closing the division:
options: Makes the company Rs.1L/month WORSE off
questions.why: If closed: Revenue 0, Avoidable 0, Unavoidable still -Rs.4L/month. Closed = -Rs.4L vs Open = -Rs.5L. Closing makes things Rs.1L worse. Keep open.

questions.q: CS Ratio = 45%. Fixed Costs = Rs.9,00,000. Break-even sales value is:
questions.why: BEP Sales = FC / CS Ratio = 9,00,000 / 0.45 = Rs.20,00,000.

questions.q: Two products: X (CM Rs.60, 700 units), Y (CM Rs.100, 300 units). Total FC Rs.70,000. Are we above or below break-even?
questions.why: Total contribution = (60x700)+(100x300) = 42,000+30,000=72,000. FC=70,000. Profit=Rs.2,000. ABOVE break-even.

questions.q: The Prestige case teaches managers that before shutting a division, they should ask:
options: What are avoidable costs vs revenue lost, and what is the net financial impact?
questions.why: The correct question = relevant cost analysis: will closing make me BETTER or WORSE off financially?

questions.q: Advertising spend of Rs.40,000 increases contribution by Rs.55,000. Net impact on profit:
questions.why: Net = Incremental Contribution - Incremental Cost = 55,000 - 40,000 = +Rs.15,000. ACCEPT.

questions.q: If a company's CS ratio is 30% and it wants to earn Rs.90,000 profit with FC of Rs.2,10,000, required sales are:
Sales Rs.300L, COGS Rs.180L, Operating Exp Rs.60L, Interest Rs.15L, Tax Rs.15L. Gross Profit Margin:
Using Q41: Operating Profit Margin:
Using Q41: Net Profit Margin:
questions.why: PAT = OP - Interest - Tax = 60-15-15=30. NPM = 30/300 = 10%.

questions.q: Total Assets Rs.400L, PAT Rs.30L. ROTA (using PAT as approximate, no interest/tax data given):
questions.why: ROTA = PAT / Total Assets = 30/400 = 7.5%. (Note: strictly ROTA uses PBIAT. When interest and tax data are not given, PAT/Total Assets is used as an approximation.)

questions.q: Capital Employed Rs.300L (Equity Rs.200L + LT Debt Rs.100L), PAT Rs.30L. ROE is:
questions.why: ROE = PAT / Equity = 30/200 = 15%. Note: ROE (15%) > ROTA (7.5%) demonstrates positive leverage effect.

questions.q: ROE = PAT / Net Worth = 30/200 = 15%. ROTA = PAT / Total Assets = 30/400 = 7.5%. The pattern ROE > ROTA shows:
options: Positive leverage -- debt is amplifying returns to equity holders
questions.why: ROE (15%) > ROTA (7.5%). The debt in the capital structure is working in favour of equity holders.

questions.q: Days Inventory Outstanding: 40 days. Days Sales Outstanding: 30 days. Days Payable Outstanding: 60 days. CCC:
questions.why: CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO = 40 + 30 - 60 = 10 days.

questions.q: Company A: CCC = -15 days. Company B: CCC = +45 days. Who manages working capital better?
options: Company B -- more positive is safer
Company A -- negative CCC means suppliers fund operations
questions.why: Negative CCC = collect cash before paying suppliers = free funding = excellent working capital management.

questions.q: A company's ROTA = 12% and interest rate on new debt = 9%. Should it take more debt?
options: Yes -- ROTA > cost of debt creates positive leverage, amplifying ROE
Only if current ratio is above 2.0
questions.why: ROTA (12%) > Debt Cost (9%) = positive leverage. Extra returns go to equity holders.

questions.q: Horizontal analysis: Year 1 COGS Rs.50L, Year 2 Rs.65L. Revenue Year 1 Rs.100L, Year 2 Rs.120L. Key insight:
options: Both COGS and Revenue grew -- good news
COGS grew 30% but Revenue grew only 20% -- gross margin is shrinking
questions.why: COGS growth (30%) > Revenue growth (20%) = gross margin declining. Need to investigate cost of production.

questions.q: A company's bond (long-term debt) matures in 8 months. On the balance sheet, it should appear as:
questions.why: When long-term debt falls within 12 months of maturity, it is RECLASSIFIED as a current liability.

questions.q: An IT company acquires a manufacturing company for Rs.200 cr (book value Rs.150 cr). Post-acquisition Goodwill is:
questions.why: Goodwill = Purchase Price - Book Value = 200 - 150 = Rs.50 cr.

questions.q: A company's common-size P&L shows: COGS 55%, Operating Expenses 25%, Interest 5%, Tax 3%. Net Profit Margin:
questions.why: Net PM = 100 - 55 - 25 - 5 - 3 = 12%. All items expressed as % of sales.

questions.q: Interest Coverage falls from 8x to 2.5x over 3 years. This trend suggests:
options: Rising debt or falling EBIT -- increasing financial risk
questions.why: IC falling sharply = EBIT declining relative to interest, or interest rising faster than EBIT. Financial risk increasing.

questions.q: Company X has Debt-Equity ratio of 0.8. Company Y has 2.5 (same industry). Which carries MORE financial risk?
questions.why: Higher D/E = more debt relative to equity = more financial obligation = higher solvency risk.

questions.q: A company announces a bonus issue. Before investing based on the price increase, you should:
options: Buy immediately -- bonus always means good news
Check whether the price premium reflects genuine operational improvement or just sentiment
Wait for the next quarterly results
questions.why: Prof. Jaiswall's lesson: bonus is a SIGNAL, not a fundamental value creation event. The premium above mathematical split is sentiment-driven and transient.

questions.q: HUL's current ratio is less than 1.0. As an analyst, you should:
options: Immediately flag as high risk of default
First understand HUL's cash conversion cycle -- negative CCC means it collects before it pays, indicating market power
questions.why: Context first. HUL's negative WC = collects from retailers before paying suppliers. Negative CCC = market power. This is a STRENGTH.

questions.q: Which company would typically have the HIGHEST gross profit margin?
options: A software company selling proprietary enterprise solutions
questions.why: Software = near-zero variable cost per sale. Margins 60-80%+ typical. Steel, grocery, trading = commodity/low-margin businesses.

questions.q: ROE is 25%, ROCE is 18%, ROTA is 12%. What does this pattern tell you?
options: Positive leverage -- ROTA > cost of debt, so debt is amplifying equity returns
questions.why: ROE (25%) > ROCE (18%) > ROTA (12%) = classic positive leverage pyramid. Debt is working FOR the shareholders.

questions.q: A company improves its DPO from 30 days to 50 days (within supplier terms). CCC impact:
options: Cannot determine without DIO and DSO
questions.why: CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO. DPO increases by 20 days. Since DPO is SUBTRACTED, higher DPO = lower CCC. CCC falls by 20 days.

questions.q: A manager says: "We should close the loss-making product line immediately." As a finance-literate colleague, your FIRST response is:
options: Agree -- P&L loss is clear evidence
Ask: what are the avoidable costs vs fixed costs allocated? Will closing actually improve overall profit?
questions.why: Relevant cost thinking: the P&L shows allocated costs. The shutdown decision needs AVOIDABLE vs UNAVOIDABLE analysis.

questions.q: A startup shows a Net Loss of Rs.2L in Month 1 but positive CFO of Rs.0.5L. This MOST LIKELY means:
options: The company is in trouble despite positive cash
High non-cash charges (depreciation) and good collections make cash better than profit
questions.why: Positive CFO despite loss = non-cash charges (large depreciation) being added back. The business is operationally generating cash.

questions.q: Richie Advisors: In February, Babu pays Rs.4,000 in advance. In March, Richie does the work. Across both months, total revenue recognised from Babu:
questions.why: Revenue recognised ONCE in March when service is performed. February = Unearned Revenue (liability). Total = Rs.4,000 recognised.

questions.q: Using the contribution format, a company reports: Sales Rs.10L, Variable Costs Rs.6L, Fixed Costs Rs.3L. If sales rise by Rs.1L (all variable costs increase proportionally), new profit is:
questions.why: Current CM = 4L, Profit = 1L. CS ratio = 40%. Extra contribution from Rs.1L extra sales = 1L x 40% = Rs.0.4L. New profit = 1 + 0.4 = Rs.1.4L.

questions.q: A company has zero goodwill on its balance sheet. This means:
options: The company has no brand value
The company has not done an M&A where it paid above book value
questions.why: Goodwill on balance sheet = PURCHASED goodwill only. Zero goodwill = no qualifying M&A done. Says nothing about brand value.

questions.q: Which of the following would INCREASE Retained Earnings?
questions.why: RE = Opening RE + Net Income - Dividends. Net income INCREASES RE. Loss decreases it. Dividends decrease it. New shares increase Share Capital, not RE.

questions.q: A company has very HIGH inventory days (DIO = 120 days). This might indicate:
options: Slow-moving or obsolete inventory, or over-purchasing
questions.why: High DIO = inventory sitting for long time = potential obsolescence, poor demand forecasting, or over-purchasing.

questions.q: Which of the following would NOT appear on a company's income statement?
questions.why: Dividends are NOT an expense -- they do not go through the P&L.; They reduce Retained Earnings on the Balance Sheet.

questions.q: A company's 5-year revenue trend is: 100, 108, 118, 130, 145. Operating income trend: 100, 105, 115, 125, 150. Which trend is accelerating relative to the other?
options: Operating income growing faster (especially in Year 5)
They are growing at the same rate
questions.why: Year 5: Revenue index 145, Operating income index 150. Operating income growing faster = improving profitability per rupee of sales.

questions.q: Fixed costs Rs.2,00,000, Variable Cost per unit Rs.30, Selling Price Rs.80, actual sales 6,000 units. Margin of Safety ratio is:
Richie's February net loss is Rs.74,900 on initial capital of Rs.10L. As a shareholder, should you panic?
options: Yes -- a Rs.74,900 loss is catastrophic
No -- February was a setup month. March showed 11x revenue growth. Owners equity still Rs.9.25L.
Yes -- the loss means the business model is broken
Only if the second month also shows a loss
questions.why: Context: Rs.74,900 loss on Rs.10L capital = 7.5% in Month 1. February costs were almost entirely fixed startup costs. March validated the business model completely.

questions.q: A lender evaluating whether to give a 5-year loan would MOST focus on:
options: Interest Coverage and DSCR (long-term debt serviceability)
questions.why: Lender's concern: will I get my principal and interest back? Long-term: DSCR and Interest Coverage.

questions.q: Which statement about the Cash Flow Statement is TRUE?
options: It is easier to manipulate than the P&L
Cash in the bank is a fact -- it is harder to manipulate than accrual profit
CFO should always be negative for a growing company
questions.why: Cash is a fact. Accrual accounting involves judgment. This is why cash flow is crucial for fraud detection.

questions.q: Company A's trend: current ratio rising, inventory days rising, debtors days rising. This is:
options: Concerning -- rising liquidity ratio driven by deteriorating asset quality (slow moving stock, slow collecting)
questions.why: Higher current ratio driven by higher inventory days (slow-moving stock) and higher debtors days (slow collections) = quality of current assets is deteriorating.

questions.q: A product's CS ratio is 60%. If fixed costs increase by Rs.1,20,000, the break-even sales increase by:
questions.why: BEP Sales = FC / CS Ratio. Increase in BEP Sales = 1,20,000 / 0.60 = Rs.2,00,000.

questions.q: A company's debt-equity ratio is 2.0. For every Rs.100 of equity, total assets funded by debt are:
questions.why: D/E = 2.0 means Rs.200 debt per Rs.100 equity. Total capital = 200+100=300. Debt = Rs.200.

questions.q: Prestige Data Services idle hours fell from 223 (Jan) to 143 (Mar). Commercial hours rose from 123 to 138. The BEST conclusion for Daniel Rowe is:
options: Continue -- trend is clearly positive; need only 45 more commercial hours/month to break even
questions.why: Direction: losses narrowing, commercial hours rising, idle hours falling. Gap to break-even = 45 hours/month. Specific, achievable target.

questions.q: Which ratio measures "for every rupee of equity invested, how much profit did equity holders earn"?
questions.why: ROE = PAT / Net Worth (Equity). Directly measures return on equity holders' investment.

questions.q: In year 1: Profit Rs.50L, Depreciation Rs.15L, Capex Rs.80L. In year 5: same profit, depreciation Rs.25L, Capex Rs.20L. Which year has BETTER cash quality?
options: Year 5 -- same profit but lower capex and higher depreciation add-back = higher free cash flow
questions.why: Year 5: CFO approx 50+25=75L. Capex Rs.20L. Free cash flow approx Rs.55L. Year 1: CFO approx 65L, Capex Rs.80L. Negative free cash flow. Year 5 = far better cash quality.

questions.q: A company earns Rs.1,000 revenue. COGS Rs.600. Selling expenses Rs.100. Admin expenses Rs.80. Interest Rs.30. Tax rate 30%. PAT is:
A trading company pays Rs.5 lakhs as a refundable security deposit. Impact on the accounting equation:
options: Total assets decrease Rs.5L; OE decreases Rs.5L
Cash decreases Rs.5L; Security Deposit (asset) increases Rs.5L -- total assets unchanged
Total liabilities increase Rs.5L; total assets increase Rs.5L
OE decreases and liabilities increase, both by Rs.5L
questions.why: The deposit is REFUNDABLE -- future benefit = Asset. Cash (asset) OUT, Security Deposit (asset) IN. Both on the LEFT side. Net change to the equation = zero.

questions.q: Which accounting principle governs recording salary payable of Rs.2 lakhs not yet paid in cash?
questions.why: Accrual Concept: record the expense when the obligation is INCURRED (employees worked this month), not when cash is paid.

questions.q: A company earns net profit Rs.4.8L and pays dividends Rs.1L. How does this flow across statements?
options: Net profit appears in CFO; dividends reduce balance sheet asset
Net profit feeds into Retained Earnings on the balance sheet; dividends reduce Retained Earnings
Net profit reduces liabilities; dividends increase OE
Net profit increases cash directly; dividends are income in P&L
questions.why: Sequence: P&L Net Profit INCREASES Retained Earnings (Owners Equity on BS). Dividends DECREASE Retained Earnings directly. They are NOT an expense on the P&L.;

questions.q: Which is correctly classified on a balance sheet?
options: A 5-year bond purchased 3 months ago is non-current
Salary payable is a long-term liability
Creditors for goods on 60-day credit are current liabilities
questions.why: Trade creditors on 60-day terms = settled within the operating cycle = CURRENT LIABILITY. Share capital = Owners Equity, not an asset.

questions.q: Company A depreciates machinery over 3 years (SLM); Company B over 5 years (SLM). Same cost, zero residual. In Year 2, Company A vs Company B:
options: Higher net profit and higher net asset value
Lower net profit AND lower net asset value
Lower net profit but identical net asset value
Higher net profit but lower net asset value
questions.why: A: dep = 10/3 = Rs.3.33L/yr. B: dep = 10/5 = Rs.2L/yr. A charges MORE depreciation = LOWER profit. A has MORE accumulated dep = LOWER NBV. Both metrics worse for A in Year 2.

questions.q: In the Six Friends case, closing cash is Rs.39L yet profit is only Rs.4.8L. PRIMARY reason:
options: Capital raised from equity (Rs.30L) and debt (Rs.20L) are in cash but NOT in profit
questions.why: Rs.50L of FINANCING inflows (equity + loan) appear in the bank balance but never in the P&L.; Profit and cash measure completely different things.

questions.q: Under WDV vs SLM, TOTAL depreciation over the full asset life is:
questions.why: Both methods depreciate (Cost minus Residual Value) in total. The only difference is TIMING -- WDV front-loads it, SLM spreads it equally.

questions.q: TTK Inc. Opening Assets $280K, Liabilities $120K. New capital $40K, dividends $48K. Closing Assets $400K, Liabilities $140K. Net income is:
questions.why: Opening OE = 160K. Closing OE = 260K. Change = +100K. NI = 100K + 48K - 40K = $108,000. Must strip out new capital and add back dividends.

questions.q: NTPC: net profit fell 19% despite operating margin expanding to 26.6%. Best explanation:
options: Higher interest, depreciation, and lower other income compressed profit below the EBIT level
Higher tax rates offset gross margin improvement
A one-time gain inflated prior year profit
questions.why: Operating margin UP = better core business. But BELOW EBIT: interest, depreciation, and lower other income drag net profit down. Classic multi-step income statement divergence.

questions.q: Which item would NOT be included in "Operating Expenses" for a manufacturing company?
questions.why: Interest expense is a FINANCING decision, not an operational one. It sits BELOW Operating Profit (EBIT) in the multi-step format. That is why EBIT = Earnings Before INTEREST and Tax.

questions.q: Infosys: "Profit for the period" Rs.14,702 cr vs "Total Comprehensive Income" Rs.14,781 cr. The Rs.79 cr difference is:
options: OCI -- fair value changes and remeasurements not routed through P&L
questions.why: OCI (Other Comprehensive Income) captures items that bypass the regular P&L -- fair value changes, actuarial gains/losses. Total Comprehensive Income = PAT + OCI.

questions.q: For HDFC Bank, which is "Revenue from Operations" (core operating income)?
options: Profit on sale of branch building
Interest income from loans advanced to customers
questions.why: For a bank, LENDING is the core business. Interest income on loans = Revenue from Operations. The others are gains, other income, or treasury activity.

questions.q: Under Schedule III (Indian GAAP), "Capital Work in Progress" is classified as:
questions.why: CWIP is a fixed asset under construction -- it will become a productive asset once commissioned. Non-Current Asset. No depreciation until ready for use.

questions.q: MTNL: Working Capital = -Rs.1,121 cr. Vodafone = +Rs.4,273 cr. Negative WC for MTNL signals:
options: Potential short-term liquidity stress -- CL exceed CA
MTNL efficiently deployed capital into long-term assets
questions.why: Negative WC = current liabilities exceed current assets. For HUL or Amazon this is market power. For MTNL with declining revenues -- liquidity stress. Context is everything.

questions.q: Infosys: Share Capital Rs.2,076 cr, Other Equity Rs.85,256 cr (ratio 1:41). Other Equity primarily represents:
options: Accumulated retained earnings built over decades of profitable operations
questions.why: Infosys has been profitable since 1981. Decades of retained earnings compound into "Other Equity." Share Capital stays at the par value of original issuance.

questions.q: Company uses WDV for tax, SLM for financial statements. In EARLY years:
options: Tax dep < Book dep → lower taxable income → Deferred Tax Asset
Tax dep > Book dep → lower taxable income → Deferred Tax Liability
Tax dep > Book dep → higher taxable income → Deferred Tax Asset
Tax and book depreciation always equal
questions.why: WDV gives HIGHER depreciation in early years. Tax dep (WDV) > Book dep (SLM) → lower taxable income today → less tax paid today → Deferred Tax LIABILITY (future obligation).

questions.q: CASE: Fortis Healthcare -- Net sales Rs.512 cr, operating margin 9.1%, interest Rs.66 cr, depreciation Rs.83.8 cr, loss before tax Rs.90 cr. Structural issue:
options: Revenue too low to be viable
Debt servicing and depreciation exceed operating profit -- over-leverage relative to revenue
questions.why: EBIT = 512 x 9.1% = Rs.46.6 cr. Interest alone = Rs.66 cr, which EXCEEDS EBIT. Even before depreciation, debt servicing kills the profit. Classic over-leveraged infrastructure acquisition.

questions.q: CASE: Power Grid -- CFO Rs.6,402 cr, CFI -Rs.15,834 cr, D/E ratio 2.1. Strategic reading:
options: Financial distress -- investing outflows far exceed operating inflows
Aggressive infrastructure expansion, funded through debt and operations -- consistent with a regulated utility
questions.why: Regulated utilities have GUARANTEED returns on infrastructure investment. High capex funded by stable CFO and debt = the business MODEL. Not distress -- disciplined expansion.

questions.q: CASE: Six Friends -- buys Rs.60L inventory, sells Rs.40L worth (cost) for Rs.50L. Gross margin and closing inventory:
questions.why: Revenue Rs.50L. COGS = Rs.40L (cost of goods SOLD). GP = Rs.10L. Margin = 10/50 = 20%. Closing inventory = 60L bought - 40L sold at cost = Rs.20L.

questions.q: CASE: IndusInd Bank Rs.1,960 cr derivative accounting error; 27% crash. Which principle was violated?
options: Full Disclosure and Fair Presentation -- positions not properly valued or disclosed
questions.why: Derivatives have measurable value (mark-to-market). The violation was NOT disclosing or properly valuing them. Financial statements must faithfully represent the true position.

questions.q: CASE: Coal India EPS Rs.15.2, IPO price Rs.225. P/E = 14.8x vs sector average 12x. Implication:
options: Priced at PREMIUM to peers -- market expects higher growth or scarcity premium
P/E above average always indicates manipulation
questions.why: P/E > sector average = premium pricing. Reasons: Coal India is the only large investable coal company (scarcity), government backing, or expected earnings growth.

questions.q: CASE: Acme Consulting -- Transaction 5 shows +$5,000 cash +$5,000 AR +$10,000 OE (Revenue). Student says profit = $10,000. Correct?
options: No -- salaries, rent, utilities must be deducted from revenue
Yes -- OE increased $10,000 so profit is $10,000
questions.why: Revenue is the TOP LINE. Profit = Revenue MINUS ALL EXPENSES. One transaction cannot tell you profit. You need the full P&L for the period.

questions.q: CASE: IOCL PBT fell 70% while revenue fell only 2.4%. Most likely reason:
options: Massive increase in cost of materials squeezed margins despite stable revenues
questions.why: Revenue -2.4% but profit -70% = extreme margin compression. For a petroleum refiner, crude oil is 60-70% of revenue. Even a small input cost rise wipes out thin margins.

questions.q: CASE: HUL Goodwill Rs.17,316 cr + Intangibles Rs.27,900 cr (exceeding current assets Rs.16,049 cr). Analyst risk:
options: No risk -- intangibles are more valuable for FMCG
Goodwill and intangibles may be IMPAIRED if acquisitions underperform -- wiping out reported equity
Large intangibles mean dividends will always be higher
questions.why: Goodwill is tested for impairment annually. If acquired businesses underperform, write-down directly reduces Owners Equity. Analyst must ask: are the acquired brands actually performing?

questions.q: Company reports assets at historical cost despite market value appreciation. Justification:
questions.why: Historical Cost: assets recorded at original cost, not revalued upward. Ensures objectivity and verifiability.

questions.q: Asset life was 10 years (SLM). After 4 years, revised to 3 more years (not 6). Accounting impact:
options: Revised estimate applied PROSPECTIVELY -- higher annual dep going forward, no restatement
No change -- only affects disposal entry
questions.why: Changes in accounting ESTIMATES are PROSPECTIVE only. Take current NBV, spread over revised remaining life. No restatement of prior statements.

questions.q: A credit rating agency evaluating debt downgrade needs which statement MOST?
options: Cash Flow Statement -- CFO and debt service coverage
questions.why: Rating agencies care: can this company PAY ITS DEBT? That requires CASH, not just profit. CFO and DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio) are the primary tests.

questions.q: RIL issues equity Rs.5,000 cr and uses proceeds to acquire a competitor. CFS classification:
questions.why: Equity issuance = raising FUNDING = Financing Activity (CFF). Acquisition of a company = deploying into a long-term asset = Investing Activity (CFI).

questions.q: Net profit grew 30%, Cash from Operations fell 15%. Most concerning interpretation:
options: Possible earnings manipulation through aggressive revenue recognition or understated provisions
questions.why: Profit up, cash down = widening accrual-cash gap. Red flag: revenue recognised before earned, or provisions understated. One of the earliest fraud signals.

questions.q: Nestle income statement: "Changes in Inventories: -Rs.627 cr." This means:
options: Inventory INCREASED -- excess cost deferred to balance sheet
Raw material consumption less than purchases
questions.why: When inventory INCREASES, company produced MORE than it sold. Unsold production cost is NOT charged to P&L -- deferred to balance sheet as inventory (asset). The -627 adjustment REDUCES cost charged this period.

questions.q: Owner's equity is best described as:
options: Residual interest in assets after deducting all liabilities
Sum of all dividends paid historically
questions.why: OE = Assets minus Liabilities. The RESIDUAL belonging to owners after all outsiders (banks, suppliers) are paid. Includes Share Capital plus Retained Earnings.

questions.q: Asian Paints: EBITDA Rs.7,855 cr, Revenue Rs.30,850 cr (25.5% margin), Raw materials Rs.13,418 cr. If raw materials rise 10%, new EBITDA margin is approximately:
questions.why: RM increase = 13,418 x 10% = Rs.1,342 cr. New EBITDA = 7,855 - 1,342 = Rs.6,513 cr. New margin = 6,513 / 30,850 = 21.1% ≈ 21.2%. A 10% raw material rise cuts margin by 4.4 percentage points.

questions.q: Company records salary expense Rs.2L as payable (not yet paid in cash). Effect on accounting equation:
options: Assets decrease Rs.2L; Liabilities increase Rs.2L
Assets unchanged; Liabilities increase Rs.2L; OE decreases Rs.2L
Assets decrease Rs.2L; OE decreases Rs.2L
Liabilities decrease Rs.2L; OE increases Rs.2L
questions.why: No cash leaves (assets unchanged). Obligation arises (Salary Payable = Liability +Rs.2L). Expense reduces OE (Retained Earnings -Rs.2L). Equation: both sides of the right side move, netting to zero change.

questions.q: RIL Non-Current Investments Rs.3,01,400 cr in standalone but largely disappear in consolidated. Why:
options: Intercompany investments eliminated against subsidiaries' equity; actual assets and liabilities reported instead
RIL writes off investments in acquisition year
questions.why: Consolidation combines parent and subsidiaries as ONE entity. Parent's investment in subsidiary is eliminated against the subsidiary's equity. Actual assets, liabilities, revenues of ALL entities reported directly.

questions.q: Kingfisher Airlines unable to pay debts. Auditor applying Going Concern should:
options: Continue applying since all companies are assumed ongoing
DISCLOSE in audit report that going concern may not be appropriate; assets potentially at liquidation values
questions.why: Going Concern is an ASSUMPTION that can be violated. If doubtful, auditor MUST disclose prominently. Assets then valued at forced-sale (liquidation) prices, not cost minus depreciation.

questions.q: NTPC income statement includes "Exceptional Item" Rs.1,363 cr reducing profit. Rationale:
options: Exceptional items not subject to taxation
Separating unusual, non-recurring items allows better assessment of RECURRING business performance
Must always be presented below the tax line
Regulators require items above Rs.1,000 cr to be exceptional
questions.why: Transparency: if a one-time charge is mixed into operating expenses, users overestimate the structural cost base. Separating it lets investors judge recurring profit correctly.

questions.q: Company X: Net Profit Rs.100 cr, Sales Rs.2,000 cr, Total Assets Rs.1,000 cr, Equity Rs.400 cr. ROE is:
questions.why: ROE = PAT / Net Worth = 100 / 400 = 25%. Note: Net Profit Margin is only 5% (100/2000). Leverage amplifies the equity return -- the business earns on Rs.1,000 cr total assets but only Rs.400 cr of equity holders bear that risk.

questions.q: RIL (total assets ~Rs.9.6 lakh cr) does not separately disclose a Rs.50,000 stationery expense. Convention:
options: MATERIALITY -- omission could not influence economic decisions of users
questions.why: Materiality: disclose only information whose omission could affect a reasonable user's decisions. Rs.50,000 on Rs.9.6 lakh crore of assets = 0.000005%. Immaterial.

questions.q: CASE: Tarech Corp -- Revenue $4,800, Expenses $2,450, Dividends $410. Cash $1,890, Other assets $1,000, Payables $450, Common Stock $500. Balance sheet total:
CASE: Startup CFO chooses between SLM and WDV for delivery vehicles (Rs.10 cr, 5-yr, residual Rs.1 cr) to attract equity investors. Strategically preferable:
options: WDV -- higher early depreciation conserves cash
SLM for financial statements (higher reported profit attracts investors); WDV separately for IT filing (cash tax savings)
WDV -- produces same profit as SLM in all years
questions.why: KEY INSIGHT: Indian companies can use DIFFERENT methods for financial statements (Companies Act) and tax returns (Income Tax Act). SLM in books = higher profit = better P&L for investors. WDV in IT return = lower taxable income = real cash tax savings. Best of both worlds.
